results.content: # Understanding Gender Beyond the Binary: The Role of Intersectionality. Today’s understanding of gender challenges us to move beyond these traditional categories and embrace a more inclusive approach that recognizes the rich diversity of human identity. By exploring intersectionality—the interconnected nature of social identities—we can better understand how gender intersects with race, class, sexuality, and other aspects of our lives to create unique experiences for each individual. * How intersectionality applies to gender. Similarly, limiting gender to just two categories overlooks the rich diversity of how people actually experience and express their gender identity. To truly understand gender in all its complexity, we need a framework that can account for the multiple, overlapping identities that shape our experiences. ### How intersectionality applies to gender. When we apply intersectionality to gender studies, we recognize that no one experiences gender in isolation. **Sexual orientation:** A lesbian woman’s relationship with femininity might differ significantly from that of a heterosexual woman, as she navigates expectations around gender performance in different social contexts. **Age and generation:** Older and younger people may have different relationships with gender norms, influenced by the historical periods in which they came of age and the changing social attitudes they’ve witnessed. When we recognize that people hold multiple, intersecting identities, we can better understand why one-size-fits-all approaches to gender equality often fall short. **Greater inclusion:** By recognizing gender diversity and intersectional experiences, we can create more welcoming environments in schools, workplaces, and communities. Instead of asking “How does gender affect this situation?” we might ask “How do gender, race, class, and other identities interact to shape this experience?” Instead of assuming that all women or all men share the same concerns, we can recognize the diversity within these groups. **What do you think?** How might your own intersecting identities shape your experience of gender? 5. results.title: Beyond binary gender — Fighting Talk
results.content: # Beyond binary gender. Growing up, I thought there were only two genders. I thought you could be a man or a woman. And I thought that your gender (what you know and feel yourself to be) was almost always the same as the sex you were assigned at birth. There’s a huge, diverse gender spectrum. ## Gender isn’t binary. Sure, you can be a man, or a woman. But those aren’t the only genders. * or a whole host of other gender identities. ## Trans isn’t a gender. Being trans or cis isn’t a gender. As my friend Max says, “trans isn’t my gender, trans is **how I got here.”**. ## **What cisgender means**. For example, if you’re a cisgender man:. * You know and feel yourself to be a man (that’s your gender identity). * You were assigned male at birth (that’s your sex – although it’s not a simple binary of male versus female as many of us were taught). Your gender is “on the same side as” the sex you were assigned at birth. You’re cisgender, or cis. ## What transgender means. If you’re a transgender woman:. * You know and feel yourself to be a woman (that’s your gender identity). * You were assigned male at birth (that’s your sex). Your gender is “on the other side as” the sex you were assigned at birth. You’re transgender, or trans. ## Gender beyond the binary is global. I learned about gender as a binary: men versus women. And from the way I saw gender represented in books, TV and movies, you’d think that binary gender ruled the world. Gender beyond the binary isn’t new, and it’s not uniquely Western. “What is new is the heightened awareness of gender diversity and the transgender community because of increased media attention in recent years.”. “Colonization oppressed gender and sexual minorities” says Brenna Miairia Kutch. “These are often treated as new-fangled "Western" identities but they are far older and more diverse. There is so much gender diversity, and so much queer identity, around the world. If we only see the binary, we’re missing a world of joy, beauty and humanity. ## What intersectionality means Next.

results.title: Beyond the Binary: Improving Data Visualization for Intersectional Identities | Nightingale
results.content: # Beyond the Binary: Improving Data Visualization for Intersectional Identities. These identities intersect across categories like gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, and socioeconomic status, creating complex and multifaceted social realities. By leveraging flexible data categories and creating models that reflect the dynamic nature of identity, data visualization can play a critical role in advancing equity and inclusion. Intersectionality is vital to socially focused research because it reveals how unique experiences emerge from the intersections of identities, rather than from individual categories like race or gender in isolation. Over the years, I have explored the academic literature, engaged with professional communities/listservs, and even turned to popular forums like *r/dataisbeautiful* in search of effective ways to visualize and represent intersectional data. **Statistical modeling.** In quantitative research, studying intersectionality means understanding how overlapping social identities combine to shape experiences, rather than analyzing them separately. Multilevel models provide another way to explore intersectionality by separating the effects of broader social categories (such as race or socioeconomic status) from individual differences. To address these challenges, it is essential for data analysts to clearly explain the graph’s purpose and limitations, ensuring that viewers understand what the visualization represents—and what it does not. This sequential approach highlights the distribution of individuals across these intersecting categories, offering both a numerical and visual understanding of how these groups overlap. These tables provide a clear and straightforward way to examine how categories intersect without overcomplicating the visualization. Yet, I find that this last approach provides a flexible framework for exploring intersectional data in a way that is both interpretable and grounded in real-world contexts. In exploring ways to better visualize intersectional data, I’ve experimented with several techniques that, while conceptually interesting, ultimately failed to communicate effectively. By giving voice to individuals from specific intersectional identities, this method allows them to articulate their unique experiences and needs in a way that no graph or chart ever could. Some visualization techniques can offer partial solutions by highlighting overlapping identities, but these methods often rely on simplifying assumptions or produce unwieldy outputs that fail to fully capture the richness of intersectional data. Visualizing intersectional data is inherently difficult because it requires representing the intricate relationships between multiple, interwoven categories.

results.title: Beyond the Gender Binary - UN Today
results.content: Published Time: 2020-04-09T16:23:00+00:00 Beyond the Gender Binary - UN Today ### Beyond the Gender Binary ##### As the UN system looks to reform and make efforts for a more inclusive and diverse work force, what will this mean for the most unrepresented members of society in particular gender diverse persons? BY ****Gurchaten Sandhu**** | 9 April 2020 #### _As the UN system looks to reform and make efforts for a more inclusive and diverse work force, what will this mean for the most unrepresented members of society in particular gender diverse persons? Yet as the UN system looks to reform and make efforts for a more inclusive and diverse work force, what will this mean for the most unrepresented members of society, in particular gender diverse persons? Within the UN System, trans, non-binary and gender diverse identified staff have experienced being victims of harassment, or have faced an Organization that does not know how to account for their gender identity, or desires to change their gender identity and undergo transition. Trans and non-binary persons frequently inform UN GLOBE of the issues they have accessing UN Offices around the world, including Offices based in countries with more progressive gender identity laws in place. In order to capacitate the UN system to meet the needs of trans-identified individuals, and under the overarching goal of a more diverse, more inclusive UN system, UN-GLOBE developed UN-GLOBE Recommendations for an inclusive workplace for trans and gender non-conforming staff members, dependents, and other stakeholders of the UN System. These recommendations are intentionally comprehensive to ensure all needs of trans, non-binary and gender diverse-identified individuals are met. The Strategy cannot succeed without a change in culture— from binary gender to one of gender diversity that is inclusive of trans-identified individuals, gender non-conforming individuals, those who don’t identify with a gender, and others. UN-GLOBE stands ready to help the Organizations of the UN System implement policies that can help ensure inclusiveness for the increasing number of staff who identify as trans and gender non-conforming.**UN-GLOBE** UN-GLOBE is the inter-agency system wide group representing LGBTIQ+ staff, interns and consultants in the UN system.
